The Strata programmable valve is an adjustable cerebrospinal fluid shunt system with five performance level settings that can be adjusted noninvasively using an external magnet. The valve includes an anti-siphon device and can be verified using a hand tool or radiography.

Technical Specifications

The Strata valve has the following opening pressure settings across its five performance levels:

Performance Level 0.5: 3.3 mmHg

Performance Level 1.0: 5.1 mmHg

Performance Level 1.5: 7.7 mmHg

Performance Level 2.0: 10.7 mmHg

Performance Level 2.5: 13.1 mmHg

The mean resistance is 2.2 ± 1.0 mmHg/ml/min, with the anti-siphoning device functioning reliably across all valves tested.

Recent population-based data shows adjustable valves (including Strata) have lower overall revision rates compared to fixed-pressure valves (14% vs 30%, p<0.001). A meta-analysis found programmable valves reduced revision surgery rates (12% vs 32%) and subdural collections (9% vs 22%) compared to fixed valves.

World Federation of Neurological Surgeons grading scale

It is based on the GCS score and the presence of motor deficits.

●Grade 1: GCS score 15, no motor deficit

●Grade 2: GCS score 13 to 14, no motor deficit

●Grade 3: GCS score 13 to 14, with motor deficit

●Grade 4: GCS score 7 to 12, with or without motor deficit

●Grade 5: GCS score 3 to 6, with or without motor deficit

A systematic review of SAH grading scales found conflicting data regarding the prognostic power of the WFNS grades; two studies showed a stepwise increase in the likelihood of poor outcome with increasing WFNS grade, while others did not find consistent significant differences in outcome between adjacent WFNS grades.

Hunt and Hess grading system — The scale was intended as an index of surgical risk. The initial clinical grade correlates with the severity of hemorrhage.

●Grade 1: Asymptomatic or mild headache and slight nuchal rigidity

●Grade 2: Moderate to severe headache, stiff neck, no neurologic deficit except cranial nerve palsy

●Grade 3: Drowsy or confused, mild focal neurologic deficit

●Grade 4: Stupor, moderate or severe hemiparesis

●Grade 5: Deep coma, decerebrate posturing

A study of 230 patients with SAH found a significant difference in outcome for compressed but not adjacent Hunt and Hess grades; patients with grades 1 to 3 had better outcomes compared with those with grades 4 and 5.

A systematic review of SAH grading scales found conflicting data regarding the utility of the Hunt and Hess scale for prognosis

Modified Fisher scale — Like the Fisher scale, the modified Fisher scale (also known as the Claassen grading system) is an index of the risk of delayed cerebral ischemia due to vasospasm after SAH. It does not address clinical outcomes. Unlike the Fisher scale, the modified Fisher scale takes into account the separate and additive risk of SAH and intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH).

Ten cisterns or fissures are evaluated for blood with the modified Fisher scale. These include the frontal interhemispheric fissure, the quadrigeminal cistern, the bilateral suprasellar and ambient cisterns, and the bilateral basal sylvian and lateral sylvian fissures. The scale is graded as follows:

●Grade 0: No SAH or IVH

●Grade 1: Minimal SAH and no IVH

●Grade 2: Minimal SAH with bilateral IVH

●Grade 3: Thick SAH (completely filling one or more cistern or fissure) without bilateral IVH

●Grade 4: Thick SAH (completely filling one or more cistern or fissure) with bilateral IVH

The best predictors of delayed cerebral ischemia due to vasospasm were thick SAH completely filling any cistern or fissure (odds ratio [OR] 2.3, 95% CI 1.5-9.5) and bilateral IVH (OR 4.1, 95% CI 1.7-9.8).

Ogilvy and Carter grading system — A SAH classification system to predict outcome for surgical management of SAH due to ruptured aneurysm. It stratifies patients based upon age, Hunt and Hess grade (clinical condition), Fisher grade (SAH volume and vasospasm risk), and aneurysm size.

One point is given for each of the following variables:

●Age greater than 50

●Hunt and Hess grade 4 to 5 (in coma)

●Fisher grade score 3 to 4

●Aneurysm size >10 mm

●An additional point is added for a giant posterior circulation aneurysm (≥25 mm)

The total score ranges from 0 to 5, corresponding to grades 0 to 5.

In a prospective evaluation of this system in 72 patients with SAH, the authors reported good to excellent outcomes in greater than 78 percent of patients with grades 0 to 2. In comparison, good outcomes were seen in 67 percent of grade 3 and 25 percent of grade 4 patients. Of note, there was no statistical difference in outcomes between grades 0 and 1.

The relationship between internal carotid artery (ICA) tortuosity and stroke remains controversial, though emerging evidence suggests an association, particularly with severe tortuosity and specific stroke subtypes.

Severe kinking: A study using digital subtraction angiography found that severe kinking (but not mild or moderate) was independently associated with ischemic stroke/TIA (OR 1.39, 95% CI 1.03-1.88), with posterior circulation being particularly vulnerable.

Ipsilateral cerebral ischemia: In a large ultrasonographic study of 19,804 patients, carotid kinking was associated with ipsilateral cerebral ischemic events (OR 1.43, 95% CI 1.04-1.96). The prevalence of ICA morphological changes was 13.5%, with kinking representing 80% of cases.

Approximately 20% of intracerebral hemorrhages are caused by underlying structural lesions rather than purely small vessel rupture. The remaining 80% are primary or spontaneous ICH resulting from cerebral small vessel disease (hypertensive arteriolosclerosis or cerebral amyloid angiopathy).

Structural lesions causing secondary ICH include:

Macrovascular malformations (arteriovenous malformations, aneurysms, dural arteriovenous fistulas, cavernous malformations)

Intracranial tumors

Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis

Hemorrhagic transformation of ischemic stroke

Coagulation disorders

Mycotic aneurysms

Reversible vasoconstriction syndrome

The pathophysiology of cervicogenic dizziness (CGD) centers on sensory mismatch theory, where disrupted cervical proprioceptive input conflicts with vestibular and visual information, leading to postural instability and dizziness. This remains a controversial clinical entity, with ongoing debate about its existence as an independent diagnosis.

Primary Mechanism: Proprioceptive Dysfunction

The cervical spine contains highly developed proprioceptive receptors that normally integrate with vestibular and visual systems in the central nervous system to coordinate head, eye, neck, and body movements through various reflex activities. When cervical proprioceptive input becomes abnormal—from diseased intervertebral discs, damaged joint receptors, or tense neck muscles—this creates a mismatch with vestibular and visual sensory information, resulting in dizziness and unsteadiness.

Recent research suggests that ingrowth of Ruffini corpuscles into diseased cervical discs may contribute to abnormal proprioceptive signaling. These signals, combined with input from muscle spindles in tense neck muscles secondary to pain, are transmitted to the central nervous system where they conflict with other sensory inputs.

Central Mechanisms

Beyond peripheral proprioceptive dysfunction, central mechanisms including sensory reweighting and maladaptation complicate symptom resolution, particularly in chronic cervical dysfunction. The central nervous system's inability to properly integrate conflicting sensory information perpetuates symptoms even when peripheral cervical pathology is addressed.

Alternative Proposed Mechanisms

Four main hypotheses have been proposed to explain cervicogenic dizziness:

- Proprioceptive cervical vertigo (most widely accepted)

- Barré-Liéou syndrome: Originally proposed in 1928 involving abnormal cervical sympathetic nerve input; initially discredited but recently resurrected with evidence of noradrenergic pathways between cervical spinal and sympathetic ganglia that may affect vertebrobasilar artery flow

- Rotational vertebral artery vertigo: A rare entity involving mechanical compression of vertebral arteries

- Migraine-associated cervicogenic vertigo

Clinical Context

The diagnosis remains challenging due to the absence of specific diagnostic criteria or gold-standard tests, relying on exclusion of other causes. The association between cervical spondylosis and dizziness is particularly controversial—while some studies report high prevalence, the actual causal relationship may be weak. One study found only a 1.6% difference in dizziness incidence between cervical and lumbar spondylosis patients, suggesting cervical spondylosis is an uncommon cause of dizziness even in those with degenerative cervical disease.

The diagnostic yield of carotid duplex ultrasound in patients with isolated neck soreness/tightness and dizziness is very low, and this test is not routinely indicated for these nonspecific symptoms.

Relationship Between Carotid Disease and Dizziness

Carotid artery stenosis causes stroke primarily through thromboembolic mechanisms (plaque rupture with embolization), not through hypoperfusion-related dizziness. The Society for Vascular Surgery explicitly states that nonspecific neurologic symptoms including vertigo, ataxia, diplopia, dysarthria, syncope, and dizziness are not typically associated with carotid territory thromboembolic events.

While vertigo was associated with subsequent stroke risk in one population-based study of patients ≥65 years, a direct causative relationship to extracranial carotid vascular disease has not been established. The pathophysiological mechanism remains unclear, and isolated dizziness is not considered a typical manifestation of carotid stenosis.

Guideline Recommendations

The 2011 ACC/AHA/ASA guidelines give carotid duplex ultrasound only a Class IIb recommendation (may be considered) for patients with nonspecific neurological symptoms when cerebral ischemia is a plausible cause. This is a weak recommendation with Level C evidence, indicating expert opinion rather than strong data.

The American Academy of Family Physicians states that patients with symptoms suggestive of cardiac disease should have carotid Doppler ultrasonography, but routine imaging is not indicated for most patients presenting with dizziness.

Clinical Context

In an older study of 101 consecutive patients with dizziness, hemodynamically significant carotid disease was found in 21% overall, but notably none of the 7 patients with isolated vertigo had significant carotid disease. The yield was higher in patients with "lightheadedness" (24%), syncope (19%), or associated focal cerebral signs (26%).

However, this must be interpreted cautiously—carotid stenosis is common in older adults with vascular risk factors, and finding stenosis does not prove causation for dizziness symptoms. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends against screening asymptomatic adults for carotid stenosis.

Practical Approach

For patients with neck soreness/tightness and dizziness without focal neurological symptoms (weakness, sensory deficits, aphasia, amaurosis fugax), carotid imaging is generally not warranted. Consider carotid duplex if the patient has:

- Focal hemispheric or retinal ischemic symptoms (TIA, stroke, amaurosis fugax)

- Multiple vascular risk factors with concern for atherosclerotic disease

- Cervical bruit on examination

- Symptoms suggesting vertebrobasilar insufficiency with vascular risk factors

For isolated cervicogenic dizziness with neck pain, the evaluation should focus on cervical spine pathology, vestibular disorders, and other common causes of dizziness rather than carotid imaging.

Carotid duplex ultrasound should rarely be performed for isolated positional dizziness, as this presentation is almost never caused by carotid artery disease. The key is distinguishing benign peripheral vestibular disorders from vascular causes based on clinical features and timing.

When Positional Dizziness is NOT Vascular

Positional dizziness is most commonly benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), which has distinct clinical features:

- Brief episodes (<1 minute) triggered by specific head movements (lying down, turning over in bed, looking up)

- No spontaneous nystagmus when seated upright before positional testing

- Positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver with characteristic torsional nystagmus

- No focal neurological symptoms (no weakness, sensory deficits, diplopia, dysarthria)

- No hearing loss or tinnitus

Other common causes of positional dizziness include orthostatic hypotension, which presents with:

- Lightheadedness, visual dimming, or presyncope within 3 minutes of standing

- Symptoms relieved by sitting or lying down

- Documented BP drop ≥20 mmHg systolic or ≥10 mmHg diastolic on active stand test

- May have "coat hanger" neck/shoulder pain from muscle hypoperfusion (not vascular compression)

When to Consider Vascular Causes

Carotid imaging is not indicated for positional dizziness because:

- Nonspecific symptoms including vertigo, ataxia, diplopia, dysarthria, syncope, and dizziness are not typically associated with carotid territory thromboembolic events

- Carotid stenosis causes stroke through embolism, not hypoperfusion-related dizziness

- The carotid circulation supplies the cerebral hemispheres, not the vestibular apparatus

Vertebrobasilar insufficiency (VBI) is the relevant vascular consideration for positional dizziness, but it has distinct features:

- Spontaneous episodes (not just positional), though may be triggered by standing or head rotation

- Multiple posterior circulation symptoms: dizziness PLUS diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia, bilateral weakness, visual field defects, perioral numbness

- Usually continuous rather than brief (<30 seconds) episodes

- Nystagmus that is gaze-evoked, does not fatigue, and is not suppressed by fixation

- Risk factors: elderly, atherosclerotic disease, vertebral artery dissection

Indications for Vascular Imaging

Consider carotid duplex only if:

- Focal hemispheric or retinal symptoms: weakness, sensory loss, aphasia, amaurosis fugax

- Cervical bruit on examination

- Multiple vascular risk factors with concern for atherosclerotic disease

For suspected VBI with positional symptoms plus other brainstem deficits, consider vertebral artery imaging (CTA/MRA of neck), not carotid duplex. However, true positional VBI is rare—one study found only 4 of 14 patients referred for suspected positional VBI had reproducible symptoms with severe posterior cerebral artery flow drops on transcranial Doppler during head rotation.

Bottom Line

For patients with isolated positional dizziness and neck soreness/tightness:

1. Perform Dix-Hallpike maneuver to diagnose BPPV

2. Perform active stand test to diagnose orthostatic hypotension

3. Do not order carotid duplex unless focal hemispheric/retinal symptoms are present

4. Consider vertebral artery imaging only if multiple posterior circulation symptoms suggest VBI

The diagnostic yield of carotid duplex in this population is essentially zero, as positional dizziness is not a manifestation of carotid disease.

Persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD) is a chronic functional vestibular disorder characterized by dizziness, unsteadiness, or non-spinning vertigo lasting ≥3 months, exacerbated by upright posture, motion, and complex visual stimuli. It is the most common cause of chronic vestibular symptoms, affecting approximately 20% of patients with vestibular symptoms in general neurology clinics and up to 40% in specialized dizziness centers.

Diagnostic Criteria (Bárány Society, 2017)

All five criteria must be met:

1. Dizziness, unsteadiness, or non-spinning vertigo present on most days for ≥3 months (symptoms wax and wane, may worsen as day progresses)

2. Exacerbated by three factors: upright posture, active/passive motion (regardless of direction), and moving visual stimuli or complex visual patterns

3. Triggered by a precipitating event: acute/episodic/chronic vestibular syndromes (BPPV, vestibular neuritis), vestibular migraine, panic/anxiety disorders, mild traumatic brain injury, stroke, dysautonomia, or psychological distress

4. Significant distress or functional impairment

5. Not better explained by another disorder

PPPD replaces older diagnostic terms including phobic postural vertigo, chronic subjective dizziness, visual vertigo, and space-motion discomfort.

Pathophysiology

The pathophysiology involves maladaptive brain responses to an initial vestibular or balance disturbance that persist after the precipitating event resolves. Current models emphasize three key mechanisms:

Psychological and behavioral responses: Anxiety following vestibular injury, dependent personality traits, autonomic arousal, and increased body vigilance (conscious attention to internal cues) at the time of precipitating events initiate PPPD. Importantly, the severity of structural vestibular deficits or compensation status does not predict PPPD development—rather, psychological and behavioral responses are the primary predictors.

Altered postural control and sensory processing: Patients develop functional shifts in stance and gait (stiffened postural control, widened base of support, shorter stride length) and become overly reliant on visual inputs versus vestibular and somatosensory inputs (visual dependence). The most recent pathophysiologic model proposes prioritization of postural stability over fluid locomotion as the core mechanism.

Brain network alterations: Neuroimaging studies demonstrate decreased functional connectivity centered on the hippocampus bilaterally, extending to inferior frontal gyrus, temporal lobes, insular cortices, and cerebellar regions, suggesting diminished integration of multisensory vestibular and spatial information processing.

Notably, neuroticism may predispose to PPPD, but premorbid psychiatric comorbidities (other than dependent personality traits) are not relevant for development.

Treatment

Treatment combines pharmacological and non-pharmacological approaches, with combination therapy superior to monotherapy.

Vestibular rehabilitation therapy (VRT) is the cornerstone non-pharmacological treatment:

- Involves walking exercises, balance retraining, and visual/postural exercises tailored to individual symptoms

- Works through habituation (reducing abnormal balance signals) and promoting central compensation

- Significantly improves Dizziness Handicap Inventory (DHI) scores, with weighted mean difference of 21.84 points compared to controls

- Both customized VRT and virtual reality-based VRT are effective, though customized VRT shows superior efficacy

- Home-based VRT is as effective as hospital-based therapy and should be considered a treatment option

- Improvements seen in DHI-Physical, DHI-Emotional, and DHI-Functional subscales

Pharmacological therapy:

- SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) and SNRIs (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) are first-line medications

- Combination of SSRI plus VRT shows significantly greater improvement in DHI and Hamilton Anxiety Scale scores compared to either therapy alone

- Current evidence recommends prioritizing SSRI plus structured VRT as the treatment option for PPPD

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT):

- Addresses anxiety and mood disturbance common in PPPD

- Sertraline plus CBT shows significantly lower DHI scores at weeks 4 and 8 compared to sertraline alone

Figure 1 undefined

- Helps patients understand and cope with symptoms more easily

- Evidence for CBT is limited but promising

Other therapies: Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) has been studied but evidence remains unclear due to limited trials and small sample sizes.

Treatment Timeline: Significant improvements in quality of life, dizziness handicap, depression, and anxiety levels occur within 3 months of VRT. Benefits of combined SSRI-CBT therapy become apparent after several weeks of treatment.

Chronic use of anti-vertigo medications (meclizine, diphenidol, flunarizine) does not provide sustained benefit for dizziness and is generally not recommended. These medications should be used only for acute symptom control for several days, not as long-term therapy.

Evidence for Chronic Use

Meclizine and antihistamines: A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis found that daily enteral use of antihistamines is not superior to placebo or no medication for improving or resolving vertigo at 1 week or 1 month (low-quality evidence). While single-dose antihistamines may provide short-term relief at 2 hours, this benefit does not translate to chronic use.

Diphenidol: Limited evidence exists for chronic diphenidol use. One small study (22 patients) treated with diphenidol 75 mg/day for 4 weeks showed improvement in physical symptoms but no improvement in emotional factors or anxiety compared to betahistine. Diphenidol improved two physical factors but was inferior to anti-anxiety medications for overall symptom management in chronic vestibular patients.

Flunarizine: Evidence for chronic flunarizine use is very low certainty. While flunarizine (10 mg daily for 2-3 months) may reduce vertigo frequency and improve symptoms in vestibular migraine, the evidence comes from small studies with wide confidence intervals. Flunarizine showed efficacy specifically for vestibular migraine prophylaxis, not for general chronic dizziness. Side effects include weight gain and drowsiness.

Why Chronic Use is Harmful

Multiple guidelines explicitly discourage chronic vestibular suppressant use for several critical reasons:

Inhibition of central compensation: The American Academy of Otolaryngology states that chronic use of vestibular suppressants suppresses central adaptation/compensation to vestibular loss and can perpetuate symptoms of chronic imbalance. This is the primary mechanism by which these medications worsen long-term outcomes—they prevent the brain from naturally adapting to vestibular dysfunction.

Lack of efficacy: The Society for Academic Emergency Medicine (GRACE-3 guidelines) notes that longer use beyond several days is discouraged due to both inhibition of physiological compensation and side effects. The American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery guidelines for BPPV explicitly discourage the use of vestibular suppressants and recommend against their routine use.

Adverse effects:

- Hypersomnolence, dry mouth, urinary retention

- Anticholinergic side effects (particularly problematic in elderly)

- The American Geriatric Society recommends against using meclizine in older individuals due to anticholinergic side effects

- Cognitive impairment, memory problems, falls risk

- For flunarizine: weight gain, drowsiness

Clinical Recommendations

Acute use only: Vestibular suppressants may be reasonable for very short periods (several days maximum) to reduce acute symptoms in conditions like vestibular neuritis or Ménière's disease attacks. After initial symptom control (maximum 3 days), treatment should be tailored to the underlying etiology.

Not for BPPV: Guidelines strongly discourage vestibular suppressants for BPPV, which should be treated with canalith repositioning maneuvers (Epley maneuver).

Not for chronic dizziness: For chronic dizziness conditions like PPPD, the evidence-based treatments are vestibular rehabilitation therapy and SSRIs, not vestibular suppressants.

Exception - Vestibular migraine prophylaxis: Flunarizine (10 mg daily) may be considered specifically for vestibular migraine prophylaxis when used for 2-3 months, though evidence quality is low and side effects are common. This is a distinct indication from general chronic dizziness.

Bottom Line

Chronic use of meclizine, diphenidol, and similar vestibular suppressants provides no sustained benefit for dizziness and actively harms patients by preventing central vestibular compensation. These medications should be limited to acute symptom control for several days only. For chronic dizziness, appropriate treatments include vestibular rehabilitation, treatment of underlying conditions (e.g., SSRIs for PPPD, prophylactic medications for vestibular migraine), and physical therapy—not chronic vestibular suppressants.

Vestibular migraine is characterized by recurrent attacks of vertigo or dizziness lasting 5 minutes to 72 hours, accompanied by migraine features such as headache, photophobia, phonophobia, or visual aura. It is the most common cause of recurrent spontaneous vertigo in adults and the second most common cause of episodic vertigo overall after benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.

Prevalence

Lifetime prevalence: 1.0% to 2.7% of the general population

Clinical settings:

- 10% to 30% of patients in specialized dizziness centers have vestibular migraine as their primary diagnosis

- 1% to 3% prevalence in general population seeking care for dizziness

- 68.4% of migraine patients report vestibular symptoms, though only 15.2% meet full diagnostic criteria for vestibular migraine

Demographics: Slight female preponderance, similar to headache migraine

Underdiagnosis: A significant number of cases remain undiagnosed due to unfamiliarity with the condition or diagnostic criteria.

Clinical Presentation

Vestibular symptoms (the predominant feature):

- Spontaneous vertigo (spinning sensation)

- Positional vertigo (triggered by head position changes)

- Visually induced vertigo (triggered by complex visual stimuli or moving visual patterns)

- Head motion-induced vertigo or dizziness with nausea

- Swaying/rocking unsteadiness or nonvertiginous dizziness with nausea

Symptoms must be moderate to severe intensity (interfering with or prohibiting daily activities) and last 5 minutes to 72 hours.

Migrainous features (must accompany ≥50% of vestibular episodes):

- Migraine headache with ≥2 of the following: unilateral location, pulsating quality, moderate-to-severe intensity, aggravation by routine physical activity

- Photophobia and phonophobia (sensitivity to light and sound)

- Visual aura

- Nausea and vomiting

Important clinical characteristics:

- Headache is NOT required during every attack—only ≥50% of episodes need migrainous features, which can include photophobia/phonophobia or visual aura without headache

- Attacks range from minutes to hours, with most lasting several hours

- Patients have extreme sensitivity to self and surround motion during attacks

- Interval symptoms: Many patients experience motion sensitivity and visual dependence between attacks

Diagnostic Criteria (Bárány Society/International Headache Society, 2012)

Definite vestibular migraine requires ALL of the following:

A. ≥5 episodes of vestibular symptoms (moderate-to-severe intensity, lasting 5 minutes to 72 hours)

B. Current or previous history of migraine (with or without aura per ICHD criteria)

C. ≥1 migraine feature during ≥50% of vestibular episodes: migraine headache, photophobia and phonophobia, or visual aura

D. Not better explained by another vestibular or headache disorder

Probable vestibular migraine:

- Same vestibular symptom requirements (≥5 episodes, 5 minutes to 72 hours)

- Only ONE of criteria B or C is fulfilled (either migraine history OR migraine features during episodes, but not both)

- Not better explained by another disorder

Functional Impact

Vestibular migraine causes significant disability:

- Greater headache-related disability (MIDAS scores: 40.9 ± 48.9 in vestibular migraine vs 23.6 ± 36.4 in migraine without vestibular symptoms)

- Poorer sleep quality (PSQI: 10.6 ± 4.0 vs 8.6 ± 3.9)

- More anxiety symptoms (HADS-A: 9.1 ± 4.1 vs 6.9 ± 4.3)

- More depression symptoms (HADS-D: 7.1 ± 4.5 vs 5.8 ± 4.2)

Notably, even migraine patients with vestibular symptoms who do not meet full criteria for vestibular migraine still experience substantial disability compared to those without vestibular symptoms.

Differential Diagnosis Challenges

Vestibular migraine diagnosis is challenging due to symptom overlap with:

- Ménière's disease (though vestibular migraine is much more common)

- BPPV (positional vertigo occurs in both)

- Other vestibular disorders

- Headache migraine with occasional vestibular symptoms (which does not constitute vestibular migraine)

The key distinguishing features are the episodic nature (5 minutes to 72 hours), recurrent pattern (≥5 lifetime episodes), and temporal association with migraine features in ≥50% of attacks.

Practice Guideline

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends recognizing catamenial seizures as cyclic seizure exacerbation in relation to the menstrual cycle, defined as a twofold increase in baseline average daily seizure activity during a particular phase of the menstrual cycle. Diagnosis requires evaluation of a menstrual and seizure diary.

Catamenial Patterns and Timing

More than one third of postmenarchal girls and women with medication-refractory epilepsy experience catamenial seizure exacerbation. The most common seizure pattern is perimenstrual, occurring 3 days before menses and the first 3 days of menses, when progesterone levels drop in ovulatory cycles. Periovulatory catamenial exacerbation has been attributed to the midcycle surge of estrogen that is relatively unopposed by progesterone. Patients have fewest seizures during the midluteal phase in ovulatory cycles when progesterone levels are highest.

The menstrual cycle variation in steroid hormone levels and ratios correlates with the timing of seizures in catamenial epilepsy.


Catamenial Visceral Seizures: Clinical Context

While the term "catamenial visceral seizure" is not a standard classification in the medical literature, it likely refers to seizures with visceral or autonomic features (such as epigastric rising sensation, nausea, abdominal discomfort, or other autonomic symptoms) that occur in a catamenial pattern. These visceral symptoms can be part of focal seizures, particularly those originating from the temporal lobe or insular cortex.

Pathophysiology

Catamenial epilepsy affects approximately 40% of women with epilepsy and is driven by hormonal fluctuations. Three distinct patterns have been identified:

- C1 (perimenstrual): Days -3 to +3 around menstruation, related to progesterone withdrawal

- C2 (periovulatory): Around ovulation (day 14), related to estrogen surge

- C3 (luteal phase): Days 10 through day 3 of next cycle in anovulatory cycles with inadequate luteal phase

The mechanisms involve premenstrual withdrawal of anticonvulsant neurosteroids (particularly allopregnanolone, a progesterone metabolite), alterations in GABA-A receptor subunits, and the neuroexcitatory effects of estrogen.

Treatment Approaches

Treatment depends on whether menses are regular or irregular:

For regular menses:

- Clobazam: 20-30 mg nightly for 10 days starting 2 days before expected seizures (78% response rate in one study)

- Natural progesterone: 200 mg three times daily on days 14-25 for women with ≥3-fold increase in perimenstrual seizures (37.8% responders vs 11.1% with placebo in severely affected women)

- Acetazolamide: 250-500 mg daily from 3-7 days prior to menses

- Dose adjustment: Temporary increase in baseline antiepileptic drugs during vulnerable periods

For irregular menses:

- Oral contraceptives to regulate cycles and make seizures more predictable

- Medroxyprogesterone acetate (Depo-Provera) or GnRH analogues for menstrual suppression in severe, refractory cases

Diagnostic Approach

When catamenial epilepsy is suspected, maintain a seizure and menstrual diary for at least 3 menstrual cycles to establish the pattern and relationship to menstrual phases. This documentation is essential for determining the appropriate treatment timing and approach.

This critical new information—that all episodes occur on menstrual days 1-2—substantially changes the differential diagnosis. This pattern strongly suggests catamenial vasovagal syncope (menstruation-triggered reflex syncope) rather than catamenial epilepsy, though both remain in the differential.

Most Likely Diagnosis

Catamenial vasovagal syncope (menstruation-triggered reflex syncope)

The presentation combines classic features of vasovagal syncope with a striking menstrual pattern:

- Stereotyped prodrome: Abdominal pain → diarrhea → syncope within 3 minutes is the classic autonomic prodrome of vasovagal syncope

- Rapid recovery: Complete recovery in 1-2 hours without prolonged confusion strongly favors syncope over seizures (seizures typically cause >30 minutes of postictal confusion)

- Situational triggers: Morning occurrence after long rides suggests dehydration/volume depletion as a predisposing factor

- Menstrual timing: Both vasovagal syncope patients and healthy women report greatest lightheadedness during menses, with severity scores of 53-56 during menstruation versus 41-44 during the follicular phase

The consistent occurrence on days 1-2 of menses likely reflects the convergence of multiple physiologic stressors: hormonal changes (progesterone withdrawal), menstrual-related GI symptoms (prostaglandin-mediated cramping and diarrhea), and volume depletion from both menstruation and post-travel dehydration.

Other Diagnoses to Consider

Catamenial visceral (autonomic) epilepsy

While less likely given the rapid recovery, this cannot be excluded without EEG documentation:

- Catamenial epilepsy affects ~40% of women with epilepsy, with perimenstrual pattern (days -3 to +3) being most common

- Visceral/autonomic auras (epigastric sensation, nausea, abdominal discomfort) can occur with focal seizures, particularly temporal lobe origin

- However, the rapid recovery without postictal confusion argues strongly against this diagnosis

Cardiac arrhythmia

Cannot be definitively excluded without cardiac monitoring during an event, though the prodrome makes this less likely.

Primary dysmenorrhea with exaggerated vasovagal response

Severe menstrual cramping can trigger vasovagal syncope through pain and prostaglandin-mediated effects.

Recommended evaluation:

History refinement:

- Detailed witness account of the 6 episodes to assess for seizure features (sustained tonic-clonic activity, lateral tongue biting, prolonged confusion)

- Menstrual diary for 3 cycles documenting exact timing of symptoms relative to cycle

- Hydration status and fluid intake before long rides

- Medication review (especially NSAIDs, which can worsen GI symptoms)

Initial testing:

- 12-lead ECG if not already done to exclude long QT, Brugada pattern, or other arrhythmogenic substrate

- Orthostatic vital signs (supine, 1 min, 3 min standing) to assess for orthostatic hypotension

- Hemoglobin to assess for anemia from menstrual blood loss

Diagnostic testing to distinguish syncope from seizure:

Given the infrequent nature (6 episodes in 3 years, all during menses), the following approach is recommended:

- Tilt-table testing with simultaneous EEG monitoring is reasonable to distinguish convulsive syncope from epilepsy (Class IIa recommendation). During tilt-induced syncope, EEG shows diffuse slowing with delta waves and flat-line pattern, whereas epileptic seizures show epileptiform discharges

- Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is challenging given the predictable monthly timing. An external loop recorder or patch monitor could be worn during days 1-3 of menses for 2-3 cycles to capture events

- Routine EEG is NOT recommended for syncope evaluation unless seizure features are present (Class III: No Benefit). However, if seizure remains a concern after history review, interictal EEG may show epileptiform discharges supporting epilepsy diagnosis

- Video-EEG monitoring would be definitive if an episode could be captured, but given the infrequent and predictable timing, this is impractical unless episodes become more frequent

Red flags requiring urgent evaluation:

- Syncope during exertion (suggests cardiac cause)

- Family history of sudden cardiac death

- Abnormal ECG findings

- Prolonged post-event confusion (>30 minutes suggests seizure)

Management Considerations

If vasovagal syncope is confirmed:

- Patient education about diagnosis, triggers, and benign prognosis (Class I recommendation)

- Preventive strategies for menstrual days 1-3:

- Aggressive hydration (2-3L fluid, increased salt intake) starting 24-48 hours before menses

- Avoid prolonged standing, hot environments

- Physical counter-pressure maneuvers if prodrome occurs (leg crossing, squatting)

- Pharmacologic options if conservative measures fail:

- Midodrine 5-10 mg taken on mornings of days 1-3 of menses (Class IIa for recurrent VVS)

- Fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily during vulnerable days (Class IIb)

- NSAIDs for dysmenorrhea may help reduce GI symptoms but should be used cautiously

If catamenial epilepsy is diagnosed:

- Clobazam 20-30 mg nightly for 10 days starting 2 days before expected symptoms (78% response rate)

- Acetazolamide 250-500 mg daily from 3-7 days prior to menses

- Natural progesterone 200 mg TID on days 14-25 for women with ≥3-fold perimenstrual increase (37.8% responders in severely affected women)

This autonomic testing result—poor sympathetic modulation and poor sympathetic function with normal parasympathetic function—provides critical diagnostic information that confirms the diagnosis of catamenial vasovagal syncope with underlying sympathetic dysfunction. This pattern is well-documented in patients with recurrent vasovagal syncope and has important therapeutic implications.

Clinical Significance of the Autonomic Testing

The autonomic profile reveals a sympathetic phenotype of vasovagal syncope characterized by:

Baseline sympathetic dysfunction:

- Increased resting sympathetic activity but blunted sympathetic response to orthostatic stress is characteristic of patients with recurrent vasovagal syncope

- In one study, patients with vasovagal syncope had significantly elevated resting muscle sympathetic nerve activity (42.4 bursts/min vs 26.5 in controls), but activation during orthostatic stress was markedly blunted (5.1 vs 15.2 bursts/min increase at -50 mmHg lower body negative pressure)

- Reduced baroreflex sensitivity is also typical, both at rest and during orthostatic stress

Menstrual cycle effects on sympathetic function:

- During the luteal phase (including days 1-2 of menses), sympathetic activity normally increases in healthy women, but the transduction of sympathetic activity into vascular resistance may be impaired

- Women with premenstrual symptoms show lower plasma norepinephrine during the luteal phase compared to controls (180 vs 320 pg/mL supine, 480 vs 940 pg/mL during tilt), suggesting reduced sympathetic output or increased clearance

- The combination of progesterone withdrawal (which normally suppresses sympathetic outflow) and baseline sympathetic dysfunction creates a "perfect storm" for syncope during early menses

Pathophysiologic Interpretation

The patient's presentation represents a "low sympathetic reserve" phenotype of vasovagal syncope:

1. Baseline sympathetic impairment limits the ability to mount adequate vasoconstriction during orthostatic stress

2. Dehydration from long rides reduces venous return and central blood volume

3. Early menstruation (days 1-2) compounds the problem through:

- Prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation and GI symptoms (cramping, diarrhea)

- Hormonal shifts affecting sympathetic-vascular coupling

- Possible volume loss from menstruation itself

4. Morning timing adds orthostatic stress after overnight recumbency

5. The final trigger is abrupt sympathetic withdrawal during defecation, causing the characteristic vasovagal collapse

Management Strategy Based on Autonomic Profile

Given the documented sympathetic dysfunction, treatment should focus on augmenting sympathetic vascular toneduring vulnerable periods (menstrual days 1-3 after long rides):

First-line interventions (Class I-IIa):

1. Patient education and trigger avoidance (Class I)

- Aggressive hydration (2-3L fluid, increased salt) starting 24-48 hours before menses and after long rides

- Avoid prolonged standing, hot environments, and straining during defecation on vulnerable days

- Physical counter-pressure maneuvers if prodrome occurs (leg crossing, squatting)

2. Midodrine (Class IIa for recurrent VVS)

- Dosing: 5-10 mg taken on mornings of menstrual days 1-3, especially after long rides

- Mechanism: Alpha-1 agonist that directly addresses the sympathetic vasoconstrictor deficit

- Evidence: 43% reduction in syncope recurrence in meta-analysis

- Particularly appropriate given documented poor sympathetic function

- Contraindications: Hypertension, heart failure, urinary retention

Second-line options (Class IIb):

3. Fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily during vulnerable days (Class IIb)

- Increases blood volume through mineralocorticoid activity

- POST II trial showed 31% risk reduction in adults with moderately frequent VVS

- Monitor potassium

4. Increased salt and fluid intake (Class IIb)

- Particularly important given the dehydration trigger from long rides

Menstrual-specific considerations:

5. NSAIDs for dysmenorrhea may help reduce prostaglandin-mediated GI symptoms and vasodilation, though use cautiously as they can affect renal sodium handling

6. Hormonal cycle regulation could be considered if episodes remain frequent despite above measures, though this is not specifically addressed in syncope guidelines

Not recommended:

- Beta-blockers: Class IIb in patients ≥42 years, but Class III (not indicated) in European guidelines due to negative RCT data

- Orthostatic training: Class IIb with uncertain benefit

Immediate management:

1. ECG if not already done to exclude arrhythmogenic substrate

2. Hemoglobin to assess for anemia from menstrual blood loss

3. Orthostatic vital signs to document any orthostatic hypotension component

Treatment plan:

Given the documented sympathetic dysfunction and predictable catamenial pattern:

- Start midodrine 5-10 mg on mornings of menstrual days 1-3, particularly after long rides (can titrate dose based on response)

- Implement aggressive hydration protocol: 2-3L fluid with increased salt intake starting 24-48 hours before expected menses

1. Afferent Baroreflex Failure

Pathophysiology: Loss of sensory input from carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors to the nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS). Without this inhibitory afferent input, cortical signals (e.g., mental stress) reach the rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM) unopposed, resulting in unrestrained sympathetic activation with paroxysmal surges in muscle sympathetic nerve traffic, blood pressure, and heart rate.

Causes:

- Neck radiation for head/neck cancer (most common, ~86.5% of cases), typically appearing years after treatment due to radiation-induced fibrosis of the carotid sinus

- Bilateral carotid body tumor (paraganglioma) resection with damage to the carotid sinus nerve

- Familial dysautonomia (hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type 3)

- Rare brainstem lesions involving NTS, Guillain-Barré syndrome, carotid endarterectomy

Clinical features:

- Labile hypertension with paroxysmal surges (systolic BP up to 280 mmHg) triggered by mental stress, emotional stimuli, or physical activity

- Headache, flushing, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and emotional lability during surges

- Orthostatic hypotension (present in ~75-91% but not universal)

- Plasma norepinephrine is elevated and rises appropriately on standing (intact efferent sympathetic fibers)

Autonomic testing hallmarks:

- Absent reciprocal heart rate changes during BP fluctuations (no bradycardia with phenylephrine, no tachycardia with nitroprusside)

- Absent heart rate changes during Valsalva maneuver

- Exaggerated pressor response to cold pressor test (distinguishes from efferent failure)

- Normal postganglionic sudomotor function (except focal neck anhidrosis from direct radiation)

Treatment: Clonidine (central sympatholytic) reduced attack frequency by 81% in the original series. Management often requires both antihypertensives and pressor agents.

---

2. Efferent Baroreflex Failure (Autonomic Failure)

Pathophysiology: Damage to the sympathetic efferent neurons—either preganglionic (central) or postganglionic(peripheral)—impairs norepinephrine release at the neurovascular junction, causing insufficient vasoconstriction on standing.

This category is further subdivided:

2a. Central (preganglionic) efferent failure — Multiple System Atrophy (MSA):

- α-Synuclein deposits in oligodendrocytes (glial cytoplasmic inclusions/Papp-Lantos bodies) cause neurodegeneration of central autonomic pathways: RVLM, intermediolateral columns of the spinal cord, dorsal vagal nucleus, and hypothalamus

- Postganglionic sympathetic neurons are largely spared → plasma norepinephrine is normal or near-normal at rest

- Residual sympathetic tone is present but centrally dysregulated

2b. Peripheral (postganglionic) efferent failure — Pure Autonomic Failure (PAF) and Parkinson's disease:

- α-Synuclein deposits (Lewy bodies) in postganglionic sympathetic neurons cause peripheral sympathetic denervation

- Plasma norepinephrine is very low at rest and fails to rise on standing

- Cardiac sympathetic denervation demonstrable on MIBG scintigraphy or 18F-fluorodopamine PET

Clinical features common to both subtypes:

- Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (sustained ≥20/10 mmHg drop within 3 minutes of standing)

- Supine hypertension (in ~50%, due to denervation supersensitivity and loss of nocturnal dipping)

- Lightheadedness, visual blurring, syncope, cognitive slowing on standing

- No paroxysmal hypertensive surges triggered by mental stress (distinguishes from afferent failure)

- Blunted heart rate response to orthostatic hypotension (ΔHR/ΔSBP ratio <0.5)

- Additional autonomic deficits: bladder dysfunction, constipation, erectile dysfunction, anhidrosis

Autonomic testing hallmarks:

- Reduced or absent BP overshoot after Valsalva maneuver (phase IV)

- Reduced respiratory sinus arrhythmia

- Low plasma norepinephrine (PAF) vs. normal (MSA)

- Absent cold pressor response (unlike the exaggerated response in afferent failure)

3. Vasovagal Syncope (Functional — No Structural Nerve Disease)

Pathophysiology: Unlike the above structural disorders, vasovagal syncope occurs in patients with intact baroreflex anatomy but an abnormal reflex response. The mechanism involves:

1. Trigger phase: Orthostatic stress, pain, emotion, or visceral stimuli reduce venous return → decreased cardiac filling

2. Paradoxical response: Vigorous contraction of an underfilled ventricle overstimulates intracardiac mechanoreceptors (Bezold-Jarisch reflex) → paradoxical signal to NTS

3. Sympathetic withdrawal: Abrupt cessation of muscle sympathetic nerve activity (MSNA) → loss of vasoconstriction → precipitous BP drop

4. Vagal surge: Simultaneous parasympathetic activation → bradycardia

5. Epinephrine release: Adrenal medullary activation (not under baroreflex control) causes pallor, diaphoresis, nausea during the prodrome

Sympathetic phenotypes in vasovagal syncope:

Recent research has identified distinct sympathetic nervous system phenotypes in patients with recurrent vasovagal syncope:

- Low-pressure phenotype (systolic BP <100 mmHg): Associated with low tyrosine hydroxylase levels → reduced norepinephrine synthesis

- Normal-pressure phenotype (systolic BP >100 mmHg): Associated with increased norepinephrine transporter levels → augmented norepinephrine reuptake

Both phenotypes show below-normal norepinephrine spillover during tilt, which is consistent with the autonomic testing findings in the patient under discussion (poor sympathetic modulation and function with normal parasympathetic parameters).

In this case, brain MRA has no diagnostic value, while EEG has limited but conditional value depending on how it is used.

Brain MRA / MRI

The 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Syncope Guidelines assign a Class III: No Benefit (Level B-NR) recommendation to brain MRI/CT in the routine evaluation of syncope without focal neurological findings. This patient has no focal neurological deficits, no headache, no meningismus, and no features suggesting structural intracranial pathology. Syncope results from global cerebral hypoperfusion, not from vascular stenosis or structural brain lesions. Across 5 studies, brain MRI established a diagnosis in only 0.24% of 397 syncope patients, and CT in only 1% of 2,728 patients. A meta-analysis confirmed <1% occurrence of new neurological diagnosis within 30 days of syncope presentation.

Brain MRA specifically evaluates intracranial vascular anatomy (aneurysms, stenosis, AVM). None of these conditions produce the stereotyped catamenial pattern of abdominal pain → diarrhea → syncope with rapid recovery seen in this patient. Vertebrobasilar insufficiency can cause syncope, but would present with focal brainstem signs (diplopia, dysarthria, vertigo, ataxia), which are absent here.

EEG

The diagnostic value of EEG depends entirely on the clinical context and how it is deployed:

Routine interictal EEG — low yield (Class III: No Benefit)

A review of 7 studies found routine EEG was ordered in 52% of 2,084 syncope patients but established a diagnosis in only 0.7%. The ACC/AHA/HRS guidelines explicitly state that routine EEG recording is not recommended in syncope evaluation without specific neurological features suggestive of seizure. In this patient, the clinical features (prodrome of abdominal pain/diarrhea, rapid complete recovery without postictal confusion, situational triggers) strongly favor vasovagal syncope over epilepsy.

That said, if a routine EEG were performed and showed epileptiform discharges, this would substantially shift the diagnosis toward catamenial epilepsy. Interictal EEG has a sensitivity of 0.40 and specificity of 0.95 for seizure diagnosis—meaning a positive result nearly doubles the probability of seizure, but a negative result does not exclude it.In patients under 40 years old, the yield of epileptiform abnormalities is higher than in older patients. A sleep-deprived EEG increases yield by an additional 27-30% over a standard recording.

EEG during tilt-table testing — conditionally useful (Class IIa)

The one scenario where EEG provides meaningful diagnostic value is simultaneous EEG and hemodynamic monitoring during tilt-table testing (Class IIa, Level C-LD). This approach can definitively distinguish three entities:

- Vasovagal syncope: Diffuse brainwave slowing with delta waves → flat-line pattern (reflecting global hypoperfusion)

- Epileptic seizure: Epileptiform discharges

- Pseudosyncope/psychogenic nonepileptic seizure: Normal EEG throughout the event

However, given that this patient's episodes occur only during menses days 1-2 (6 episodes in 3 years), the likelihood of reproducing an event during tilt-table testing is low.

Yes, insular and temporal lobe seizures can closely mimic vasovagal syncope, and this is a legitimate diagnostic concern in this patient. The overlap is particularly striking with anterior insular seizures, which produce visceral/autonomic symptoms nearly identical to the vasovagal prodrome. However, several clinical features in this case help distinguish between the two.

Why Insular/Temporal Seizures Can Mimic Vasovagal Syncope

The anterior insula is the primary visceral sensory cortex and a key autonomic integration center. Seizures originating here produce:

- Visceral aura: Epigastric rising sensation, abdominal pain, nausea — nearly identical to the GI prodrome this patient describes

- Autonomic features: Heart rate changes, respiratory changes, diaphoresis, pallor

- Emotional symptoms: Fear, anguish (the "hand-to-throat" sign is characteristic)

- Laryngeal constriction and throat tightness

- Loss of consciousness if seizure propagates to temporal or frontal structures

Critically, insular epilepsy is a "great mimicker" — scalp EEG is frequently nonlocalizing or normal because the insula lies deep within the lateral sulcus, far from surface electrodes. In one study, the scalp EEG correlate of insulo-opercular seizures was often just "diffuse suppression" rather than clear epileptiform discharges. Stereo-EEG (SEEG) is often required for definitive diagnosis.

Similarly, mesial temporal lobe seizures can present with abdominal aura (epigastric rising), autonomic changes, and altered awareness that may be mistaken for presyncope followed by syncope.

Both insular and temporal seizures share the same catamenial pattern as this patient — the perimenstrual C1 pattern (days -3 to +3 of menses) is the most common catamenial seizure exacerbation pattern, driven by progesterone withdrawal reducing GABAergic inhibition. About one-third of women with focal epilepsy have catamenial seizure exacerbation.

The Diagnostic Dilemma

Several features in this patient create genuine ambiguity:

1. Morning predominance: Temporal lobe seizures characteristically occur within 1 hour of waking. Seizure cycles show strong circadian phase-locking, with many focal epilepsies showing morning peaks. However, morning is also when orthostatic stress is maximal after overnight recumbency.

2. Menses day 1-2 timing: Both catamenial epilepsy (C1 pattern) and catamenial vasovagal syncope share this exact timing window, driven by the same hormonal mechanism (progesterone withdrawal) — but acting on different targets (GABA-A receptors in epilepsy vs. sympathetic-vascular coupling in syncope).

3. Abdominal pain as prodrome: This is atypical for classic vasovagal syncope (which usually features lightheadedness, nausea, visual dimming). Abdominal pain followed by diarrhea could represent either a visceral seizure aura from the anterior insula or prostaglandin-mediated dysmenorrhea triggering a vasovagal reflex.

4. Duration of ~3 minutes: This is longer than typical vasovagal syncope (<30 seconds) but shorter than most complex partial seizures. The "chillness for 1-2 minutes" could represent either postictal autonomic dysregulation or post-syncopal sympathetic recovery.

What Argues Against Seizure in This Case

- Consistent situational triggers (long ride + morning + menses) — seizures are typically not provoked by specific external situations

- Documented sympathetic dysfunction on autonomic testing — provides a clear physiologic mechanism for vasovagal syncope

- Rapid, complete recovery without postictal confusion, aphasia, or prolonged drowsiness

- No focal neurological symptoms (no déjà vu, no olfactory hallucinations, no unilateral paresthesias, no automatisms reported)

- No tongue biting (lateral tongue biting is 94% specific for seizure)

Diagnostic Approach If Seizure Remains a Concern

Given the ambiguity, a stepwise approach is reasonable:

1. Detailed witness interview: Ask specifically about automatisms (lip smacking, picking at clothes), head/eye deviation, tonic posturing, lateral tongue biting, and duration of confusion after the event. These features would strongly shift the diagnosis toward seizure.

2. Sleep-deprived EEG: If any suspicion remains, this has the highest yield among noninvasive tests. However, scalp EEG has poor sensitivity for insular epilepsy — it may be nonlocalizing or show only diffuse suppression. A normal scalp EEG does not exclude insular seizures.

3. Brain MRI with epilepsy protocol: While routine brain MRI is not indicated for syncope, if seizure is genuinely suspected, a dedicated epilepsy-protocol MRI (thin-cut coronal FLAIR through temporal lobes and insula) could identify a structural lesion (focal cortical dysplasia is the most common substrate in insular epilepsy).

4. Ambulatory video-EEG timed to menses: Given the predictable catamenial pattern, a 7-day ambulatory video-EEG starting 1-2 days before expected menses could capture an event. At least 7 days of monitoring may be needed for ≥99% diagnostic yield.

5. Tilt-table testing with simultaneous EEG (Class IIa): If an event is provoked, the EEG pattern definitively distinguishes syncope (diffuse slowing → flat line) from seizure (epileptiform discharges).

Bottom Line

The overall clinical picture — consistent situational triggers, documented sympathetic dysfunction, rapid complete recovery, and absence of focal neurological features — favors catamenial vasovagal syncope over insular/temporal seizure. However, the morning predominance, abdominal pain prodrome, and catamenial timing are shared features that prevent absolute exclusion of a seizure etiology. A targeted witness interview focusing on automatisms and postictal confusion is the single highest-yield next step to resolve this ambiguity.

CDR® Scoring Rules

Use all information available and make the best judgment. Score each category (M, O, JPS, CA, HH, PC) as independently as possible. Mark in only one box, for each category, rating impairment as decline from the person’s usual level due to cognitive loss alone, not impairment due to other factors, such as physical handicap or depression. Occasionally the evidence is ambiguous and the clinician’s best judgment is that a category could be rated in either one of two adjacent boxes, such as mild (1) or moderate (2) impairment. In that situation the standard procedure is to check the box of greater impairment.

Aphasia is taken into account by assessing both language and non-language function in each cognitive category. If aphasia is present to a greater degree than the general dementia, the subject is rated according to the general dementia. Supply evidence of non-language cognitive function.

The Global Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR®) Score is derived from the scores in each of the six categories (“box scores”) as follows. Memory (M) is considered the primary category and all others are secondary. CDR = M if at least three secondary categories are given the same score as memory. Whenever three or more secondary categories are given a score greater or less than the memory score, CDR = score of majority of secondary categories on whichever side of M has the greater number of secondary categories. When three secondary categories are scored on one side of M and two secondary categories are scored on the other side of M, CDR=M.

When M = 0.5, CDR = 1 if at least three of the other categories are scored one or greater. If M = 0.5, CDR cannot be 0; it can only be 0.5 or 1. If M = 0, CDR = 0 unless there is impairment (0.5 or greater) in two or more secondary categories, in which case CDR = 0.5.

Although applicable to most Alzheimer’s disease situations, these rules do not cover all possible scoring combinations. Unusual circumstances occur occasionally in Alzheimer’s disease and may be expected in non-Alzheimer dementia as well are scored as follows:

With ties in the secondary categories on one side of M, choose the tied scores closest to M for CDR (e.g., M and another secondary category = 3, two secondary categories = 2, and two secondary categories = 1; CDR = 2).

When only one or two secondary categories are given the same score as M, CDR = M as long as no more than two secondary categories are on either side of M.

When M = 1 or greater, CDR cannot be 0; in this circumstance, CDR = 0.5 when the majority of secondary categories are 0.

經動脈微細血管栓塞術治療慢性疼痛

經動脈微細血管栓塞術治療慢性疼痛

告別慢性疼痛：經動脈微細血管栓塞術 (TAME) 實用指南

長期飽受關節炎、五十肩、足底筋膜炎折磨，吃藥復健卻無法斷根？醫學研究發現，慢性疼痛的元凶往往是受損組織周邊長出的「異常新生血管」與伴隨的「敏感感覺神經」。

經微細動脈栓塞術 (TAME) 是一種微創治療，透過注入暫時性栓塞藥物，精準堵住這些異常血管，讓神經萎縮，從根源消除發炎與疼痛。

一、 TAME 的兩大類型

依據疼痛部位深淺，醫師會選擇最適合的方式：

簡易型 (sTAME)：

特色：不需進開刀房，在一般門診透過超音波導引即可完成，無 X 光輻射，穿刺孔極小，便利性高。

適用部位（表淺/遠端）：手指與拇指關節炎、媽媽手 (狄奎凡氏症)、足底筋膜炎、拇趾外翻痛、腳趾蹠趾關節痛。

傳統型 (TAME)：

特色：需在醫院的 X 光血管攝影室進行，利用極細微導管與 X 光顯影揪出深層異常血管。

適用部位（深層/大關節）：退化性膝關節炎、五十肩、網球肘/高爾夫球肘、跳躍膝、慢性下背痛、肩頸痠痛、骨盆腔痛，甚至幻肢痛。

二、 誰適合做？ (病患篩選與禁忌症)

適合對象：疼痛持續超過 3 到 6 個月，且經過吃藥、復健、局部打針等「保守治療」均無效的中重度疼痛患者。

不適合對象 (禁忌症)：關節已「嚴重退化」（如膝關節第 4 期，通常需直接換人工關節）、需開刀的嚴重肌腱/半月板斷裂、局部有活動性感染、嚴重動脈硬化或腫瘤患者。

三、 術前評估：為何建議做 MRI？

在決定治療前，建議進行 MRI (核磁共振) 檢查。MRI 不僅能排除上述需要開刀的嚴重破裂，還能精準揪出 X 光看不到的隱藏發炎病灶，例如「軟骨下骨髓病變」。研究證實，若 MRI 顯示有這類發炎，接受 TAME 治療的止痛效果特別好，且術後病灶甚至會隨之縮小修復。

四、 治療感受、安全性與潛在風險

什麼是「誘發痛」？ 手術僅需局部麻醉。當藥物注入異常血管時，您平時的疼痛處會出現短暫的「發熱或痠痛感」，這稱為「誘發痛」，是好現象，代表醫師精確打擊到痛源。注射完幾分鐘內痠痛即會消失。

安全性極高：臨床證實此技術無嚴重併發症，不會造成組織壞死、肌肉萎縮或永久神經損傷。

傳統型 TAME 的特別注意事項： 相較於簡易型，傳統型 TAME 雖然精準，但因流程需求，有以下幾點輕微風險需留意：

藥物過敏反應：傳統型術中為了防止血栓，會常規施打抗凝血劑（Heparin / 肝素）；此外，使用的栓塞藥物（如 IPM/CS）本質為抗生素衍生物，兩者皆有極低機率引發輕微過敏或短暫起紅疹、發癢。

局部血腫風險：傳統型需將動脈血管鞘（較大管徑的導管）置入鼠蹊部或手腕的動脈，穿刺孔較大。若術後沒有經過足夠時間的妥善加壓止血，可能在打針部位產生局部皮下血腫，少數甚至會形成假性動脈瘤（需進一步修補）。只要配合醫囑確實加壓休息，少數的微瘀血通常在一週內即會自然消退。

五、 治療預後與恢復時程

止痛效果具備「兩階段」優勢：

快速緩解期：異常神經受阻斷，術後 1 週內即有感（例如：五十肩的夜間痛能大幅減輕）。

長期修復期：隨著發炎細胞減少，術後 1 至 6 個月內疼痛會持續且穩定地下降。

整體而言，術後半年至兩年的臨床成功率高達 70% 至 90%。透過完善的醫病溝通與術後止血照護，TAME 能幫助多數患者擺脫長期對止痛藥的依賴，重拾無痛的生活品質。

膝扭傷後的內側膝痛及後小腿痛

[簡易版] [專業版] [English] [Source]

【簡易版】

膝蓋扭傷後，為什麼內側膝蓋和小腿後面會痛？

當您的膝蓋扭傷後，如果同時感到膝蓋內側疼痛、壓痛，以及小腿後側疼痛，這通常不是單一問題，可能代表以下幾個部位的組織受傷了：
內側小腿肌肉拉傷（醫學上稱為「網球腿」）：這是最常見的原因之一。
膝蓋內側的主要韌帶受傷（內側副韌帶，MCL）。
膝蓋後方的主要韌帶受傷（後十字韌帶，PCL）。
膝蓋後內側的複雜支撐結構受傷（後內側角結構）。
什麼是這些受傷的部位？
內側副韌帶 (MCL)：位於膝蓋內側，主要負責膝蓋的穩定。
常見原因：膝蓋伸直或微彎時，膝蓋受到外側撞擊或外翻力量（例如有人撞擊您的膝蓋外側）。
症狀：通常只有膝蓋內側疼痛。如果後小腿也痛，可能合併其他地方受傷。
後十字韌帶 (PCL)：位於膝蓋中央後方，防止小腿骨過度後移。
常見原因：腳掌固定時小腿前側受到撞擊，或膝蓋過度彎曲跌倒。
症狀：通常比前十字韌帶 (ACL) 撕裂輕微，但可能在膝蓋彎曲時感到內側不適。
後內側角結構：膝蓋內側後方的一組小韌帶和肌腱，與 MCL 和 PCL 損傷常常同時發生。
內側小腿肌肉（內側腓腸肌）拉傷：俗稱「網球腿」。
常見原因：突然用力伸直膝蓋並同時腳尖上勾（離心收縮），例如跑步突然加速或跳躍時。
症狀：小腿後內側急性疼痛，有時疼痛會延伸到膝蓋內側。
醫師如何判斷？

當您同時出現內側膝蓋和小腿後側疼痛時，醫師會懷疑以下幾種情況：
MCL 韌帶受傷合併小腿肌肉拉傷。
PCL 韌帶受傷合併後內側角結構受傷。
單純小腿肌肉拉傷，但疼痛傳到膝蓋內側。
檢查方式：
理學檢查：醫師會用手檢查膝蓋穩定度（MCL 外翻壓力測試、PCL 後抽屜測試），並按壓小腿上方的內側肌肉交界處。
影像檢查：
MRI（核磁共振）：能清楚看到韌帶和肌肉的詳細損傷情況。
超音波：特別適合初步評估小腿肌肉（腓腸肌）拉傷。

【專業版】

膝扭傷後的內側膝痛及後小腿痛

膝部扭傷後，若出現後小腿疼痛、內側膝痛及壓痛的組合，最常見的損傷可能性包括：內側腓腸肌（網球腿）、內側副韌帶 (MCL)、後十字韌帶 (PCL)，或後內側角結構（包含後斜韌帶 (POL) 和半膜肌複合體）。

無痛關節鬆動術

解鎖冰封的肩膀：無痛肩關節鬆動術 (Silent Manipulation)

「Silent Manipulation」是一種強調優雅且精準的技術。與傳統需全身麻醉的激烈治療不同，此技術源自日本，著重於細膩的手法與受控的力道，能在您完全清醒且無痛的狀態下，安靜且有節奏地解開關節沾黏。

一、 適合的對象（適應症）

若您的肩膀符合以下情況，此技術能提供幫助：

活動極度受限：手向前舉不超過 100°、手無法向外旋轉，或「手摸背」高度低於腰部以下。

保守治療無效：經過 3 到 6 個月的藥物、打針或物理治療，進步仍不明顯。

嚴重影響生活：疼痛導致失眠，或因肩膀僵硬而無法穿衣、梳頭與工作。

二、 療程三階段與注意事項

1. 治療前：準備與禁忌

著裝：穿著方便露出肩膀的衣物。

交通：嚴禁自駕。治療後手臂會暫時麻痺 12 小時，請務必安排親友接送或搭乘計程車。

禁忌症：如有急性骨折、關節感染、嚴重骨質疏鬆或單側肺部手術史者，需主動告知醫師評估。

2. 治療中：舒適的體驗

在全程清醒且無痛的狀態下，醫師將執行以下三個步驟：

超音波導引神經阻斷：透過超音波導引，精準阻斷頸部神經傳導，使肩膀處於無痛狀態。

肩關節類固醇注射：注射些許類固醇至前肩關節、喙肱韌帶與三角肌下滑囊，以減少治療後的發炎性疼痛。

鬆動術（精準鬆動）：在確保安全與穩定的前提下，系統化地鬆開沾黏的關節囊。在鬆動術的過程中，您可能會聽到或感覺到「啵」、「喀啦」或「撕裂」的聲響與感覺，這是因為緊縮的關節囊結構正在被鬆解。這些聲響和感覺是預期的，並代表關節囊已成功鬆開。

3. 治療後：黃金康復期

三角巾固定：治療後會使用三角巾固定，隔天麻醉消退後即可移除。

即刻活動：移除三角巾後，需開始正常生活使用，並積極配合復健運動。

持續復健：術後 8 週內是防止再次沾黏的黃金期，需喚醒因長期停用而萎縮的肌肉。

三、 臨床數據：安全性與療效

根據大型臨床研究的追蹤數據顯示，「無痛肩關節鬆動術」具有高度的安全性和顯著的療效。

Domain00.5123

OrientationFully orientedFully oriented except slight difficulty with time relationshipsModerate difficulty with time; oriented for place at examination; geographic disorientation elsewhereUsually disoriented in time, often to placeOriented to person only
Judgment & Problem SolvingSolves everyday problems well; judgment goodSlight impairment in solving problems, similarities, differencesModerate difficulty; social judgment usually maintainedSeverely impaired in handling problems; social judgment usually impairedUnable to make judgments or solve problems

entries.title: 經期相關癲癇與血管迷走性暈厥：臨床鑑別與處置

S: 病人反覆出現短暫意識喪失或抽動，需鑑別月經相關癲癇與血管迷走性暈厥。
發作常與月經週期、睡眠不足或情緒壓力相關。
病人可能描述先有頭暈、噁心或視野變暗等前驅症狀。
家屬常觀察到抽動、臉色蒼白或短暫無反應。
臨床目標是區分神經元放電發作與自主神經性暈厥。
O: 經期相關癲癇常有週期性惡化與可能 postictal 混亂。
血管迷走性暈厥常見前驅症狀如冒汗、噁心、視野變暗，恢復較快。
癲癇發作後較常有 postictal 嗜睡、定向力不佳或肌肉痠痛。
暈厥多在站立、悶熱或情緒刺激下發生，平躺後改善。
EEG、心電圖與傾斜床測試可提供客觀鑑別線索。
A: 需以病史時間軸、前驅症狀、發作後狀態與檢查結果進行鑑別。
合併發作日誌與月經日誌可提高診斷信心並協助分型。
若呈明顯週期性惡化，需高度懷疑 catamenial seizure。
若以自主神經前驅與快速恢復為主，較支持 vasovagal syncope。
仍需排除心因性、代謝性或其他結構性神經疾病。
P: 安排 EEG/心電圖與必要時傾斜床試驗，依病因個別化治療。
教育病人記錄誘發因子與危險徵象，並進行規律門診追蹤。
癲癇者可依週期調整抗癲癇藥或考慮荷爾蒙相關策略。
暈厥者強化水分鹽分補充、姿勢訓練與誘因避免。
提供安全衛教（駕駛、游泳、單獨高風險活動）並追蹤療效。

versions.simple_zh:
月經相關癲癇與血管迷走性暈厥

有些女性會在月經前後出現「短暫失去意識」或「抽筋」的情形。這兩種情況看起來很像，但原因和治療方式截然不同，需要透過詳細記錄和檢查來區分。建議從第一次出現症狀起，記錄「發作日誌＋月經日誌」至少三個月。

什麼是月經相關癲癇？

癲癇是腦細胞過度放電引起的。部分女性的癲癇在月經前後或排卵前後會明顯增加，這與女性荷爾蒙（黃體素與雌激素）在週期中的高低變化有關，可分三型：

  • 月經前後（C1型）：月經來前後約 3 天，黃體素（一種能穩定腦細胞的荷爾蒙）急速下降，腦細胞容易過度放電。
  • 排卵前後（C2型）：排卵時雌激素高峰，使腦細胞較易興奮。
  • 整個黃體期（C3型）：月經週期不規律（如多囊性卵巢症候群）的女性，黃體素長期偏低，整個後半週期都容易發作。

什麼是血管迷走性暈厥？

暈厥（昏倒）是腦部暫時缺血造成的短暫意識喪失。月經期間特別容易發生，原因包括：

  • 月經時，子宮分泌的前列腺素（一種局部荷爾蒙）使血管擴張，血壓下降。
  • 月經出血加上脫水，使血液量減少，腦部血流不足。
  • 久站、悶熱、疼痛或突然受到強烈刺激時，神經反射過強，心跳突然變慢，血壓驟降。

兩者如何分辨？

特徵月經相關癲癇血管迷走性暈厥
發作前的感覺通常無預兆，或有短暫上腹部上衝感常有頭暈、冒汗、視線模糊、噁心等預兆
發作時的樣子全身或局部抽動，有時四肢僵直肌肉鬆軟，緩緩倒下，偶有輕微抖動
發作後的狀態意識恢復慢，可能有數分鐘至數十分鐘混亂通常幾秒至 1–2 分鐘就清醒，可能感到疲倦
與月經的關係月經前後或排卵前後明顯增加月經第 1–2 天風險最高，也可在其他時間發生

建議做哪些檢查？

  • 腦波圖（EEG）：偵測腦部是否有異常放電，確認是否為癲癇。
  • 心電圖（ECG）：排除心律問題造成的暈厥。
  • 傾斜床試驗：從躺姿快速調為站姿，觀察血壓和心跳是否驟降，確認是否為暈厥。

月經相關癲癇的治療

適用情況常用藥物說明
月經前黃體素下降型（C1型）天然黃體素（progesterone）
月經週期第 14–25 天，每日 3 次服用		補充減少的黃體素，幫助穩定腦細胞，降低發作頻率
月經前短期預防（C1型）克癇隆（clobazam，苯二氮平類短效鎮靜藥）
月經預計來前 2 天起，睡前服用共 10 天		暫時加強腦細胞的「煞車」效果；僅適用於月經週期規律者
C1 / C3型輔助治療醋氮醯胺（acetazolamide）
月經前 3–7 天開始服用		降低腦細胞過度興奮，適用於月經週期穩定者

血管迷走性暈厥的預防與治療

方法說明
多喝水、補充鹽分月經來前 1–2 天開始，每天飲水 2–3 公升，並適量增加鹽分攝取，補充血液容量，防止血壓過低
米多君（midodrine，升壓藥）月經第 1–3 天早上服用，透過收縮血管防止血壓過低
氟可體松（fludrocortisone）弱型荷爾蒙，幫助腎臟保留更多鹽分，增加血液量，降低暈厥風險

⚠ 若出現運動中發作、胸痛、頭部外傷或意識持續不清超過 5 分鐘，請立即至急診評估。
versions.professional_zh:
經期相關癲癇與血管迷走性暈厥：臨床鑑別與處置

經期相關癲癇（catamenial epilepsy）與反射性暈厥（reflex syncope，尤其月經觸發型血管迷走性暈厥）均可呈現週期性意識改變，但神經內分泌機轉與自律神經病理不同，需以分型與多模式評估精準鑑別。

經期相關癲癇三型（C1–C3）與病理機轉

型別時間窗病理機轉激素特徵
C1（Perimenstrual）月經前後（通常 Day -3 到 +3）Progesterone withdrawal 導致 allopregnanolone（GABAergic neurosteroid）急速下降，GABA-A 受體抑制減弱，皮質興奮性上升；同時 GABA-A 受體 α4/δ 亞型代償性上調，對 benzodiazepine 產生耐藥性排卵週期黃體末期，黃體素：雌激素比值驟降
C2（Periovulatory）排卵期（排卵前後各 1–2 天）Estrogen surge（未受黃體素拮抗之雌激素高峰）增強 NMDA 受體活性、抑制 GABA 合成酶、增加樹突棘密度，提高神經元興奮性LH 峰值前後，雌激素高峰而黃體素尚低
C3（Inadequate luteal phase）黃體期全程（約 Day 10 至下次月經 Day 3），見於無排卵或黃體功能不全黃體素持續低下，allopregnanolone 保護效應不足，整個黃體期均易發作；無明顯單一峰值惡化期無排卵週期（PCOS、青春期早期）

傳入失調型／傳出失調型／血管迷走性暈厥：病因學、機轉與鑑別檢查

型態典型病因核心病理生理區分檢查
傳入失調型（Afferent failure）頸部放射線治療、頸動脈竇 / 舌咽神經傳入受損壓力感受器傳入失調（baroreflex afferent failure）：壓力感受器傳入受損，血壓反射緩衝失效，交感輸出波動大自主神經反射全套、Valsalva 曲線、連續血壓圖譜、Tilt table test
傳出失調型（Efferent failure）多系統萎縮（Multiple System Atrophy, MSA）、帕金森病（Parkinson disease）、純粹自主神經失調（Pure Autonomic Failure, PAF）交感傳導及血管阻力受損（impaired sympathetic transduction and vascular resistance）：直立時無法充分血管收縮，腦灌流下降；臥立血漿去甲腎上腺素（norepinephrine）差值縮小臥立心率／血壓（≥ 3 分鐘）、血漿去甲腎上腺素（norepinephrine）（仰臥 vs 站立）、汗液軸突反射（Quantitative Sudomotor Axon Reflex Test, QSART）、傾斜床試驗（tilt table）
血管迷走性暈厥（Vasovagal）情緒壓力、疼痛、久站、熱暴露、脫水、月經前列腺素效應初期交感活化後，迷走神經反射過強（Bezold-Jarisch reflex）導致急性血管擴張＋心跳過緩，腦灌流短暫中斷Tilt table 誘發型態（同步 EEG 可排除癲癇）、姿勢生命徵象、ECG/心律監測

月經觸發血管迷走性暈厥的生理壓力疊加模型

  • 前列腺素介導的多重效應：月經期子宮內膜釋放大量 prostaglandin E2 和 F2α，除引起子宮收縮外，也誘發腸道蠕動增加（腹瀉）、全身血管擴張，及迷走神經活化，形成多重觸發。
  • 交感–血管耦合下降：黃體素撤退後，黃體期交感神經活性代償性增高，但血管壁對去甲腎上腺素的反應性（sympathetic transduction）可能下降，導致體位性調節效率降低。
  • 血容量不足：月經失血＋旅行後或長時間站立脫水，使靜脈回流（venous return）與前負荷（preload）下降，降低心臟充盈壓，增加暈厥易感性。
  • 預防性水分補充策略：建議月經預計前 24–48 小時主動攝取 2–3 L/day 水分並增加鹽分（NaCl ≥ 2 g/day），以擴充循環容積並提高靜脈張力，這是 ACC/AHA Class I 推薦的非藥物一線介入。

島葉癲癇（insula seizure）：重要偽裝者

  • 右側島葉起源之癲癇發作可高度模仿 vasovagal syncope 的自律神經前驅症狀。
  • 臨床特徵：epigastric rising sensation（上腹上衝感）、噁心、心悸、冒汗，可伴隨短暫意識改變。
  • 發作期 EEG 可能以 suppression 為主，而非典型 epileptiform discharge，易被誤診為暈厥。
  • 鑑別關鍵：postictal confusion > 30 分鐘強烈提示癲癇；暈厥通常 1–2 分鐘迅速恢復。

藥物策略（分型導向）

一、月經相關癲癇（C1–C3型）

情境藥物機轉與重點
C1型（黃體素撤退）— 週期性預防天然黃體素（natural progesterone）200 mg，每日 3 次，第 14–25 天
醋酸甲羥孕酮（medroxyprogesterone acetate）		恢復孕烯醇酮（allopregnanolone）濃度，強化 GABA-A 受體抑制；隨機對照試驗（Randomized Controlled Trial, 隨機對照試驗（Randomized Controlled Trial, 隨機對照試驗）顯示嚴重受影響 C1 患者有效率 37.8%（安慰劑 11.1%）
C1型（短期覆蓋）克癇隆（clobazam）20–30 mg 睡前，發作前 2 天起連續 10 天苯二氮平類，GABA-A 受體正向調節劑；有效率約 78%；限月經可預測者
C1/C3型輔助醋氮醯胺（acetazolamide）250–500 mg/day，月經前 3–7 天碳酸酐酶抑制劑，輕度代謝性酸中毒降低神經元興奮性

二、血管迷走性暈厥／神經性直立性低血壓

情境藥物機轉與重點
血管迷走性暈厥（VVS）／神經性直立性低血壓米多君（midodrine）5–10 mg，月經第 1–3 天清晨使用甲型腎上腺素受體促效劑（alpha-1 agonist），直接強化交感傳出不足；統合分析（meta-analysis）顯示可降低暈厥復發約 43%
血管迷走性暈厥（VVS）／神經性直立性低血壓氟可體松（fludrocortisone）0.1 mg/day，脆弱期使用礦物皮質素，增加腎小管鈉再吸收，擴充血容量；POST II 試驗顯示可降低中度頻繁暈厥復發風險約 31%；需監測低血鉀

臨床決策應先完成事件分型（seizure vs syncope）與自律神經功能分層，再進行藥物個別化。使用 EEG 結合傾斜床試驗（tilt table + simultaneous EEG）為最有效的單一鑑別工具。
versions.english:
Catamenial Seizure vs Vasovagal Syncope: Clinical Differentiation and Management

Both conditions can present with transient loss of consciousness, but endocrine seizure modulation and autonomic reflex failure follow different mechanisms and require different treatments.

Catamenial patterns (C1 to C3) and pathomechanism

PatternCycle windowPathomechanism
C1 (Perimenstrual)~Day -3 to +3 around mensesProgesterone withdrawal lowers inhibitory neurosteroid/GABA effects
C2 (Periovulatory)Ovulatory phaseEstrogen surge increases cortical excitability
C3 (Inadequate luteal phase)Luteal phase insufficiencyRelative progesterone deficiency across luteal days

Afferent failure, efferent failure, and vasovagal phenotypes

PhenotypeEtiology examplesCore mechanismTests to distinguish
Afferent failureNeck radiation, carotid sinus/baroreflex afferent injuryFailed baroreceptor input with unstable BP bufferingTilt-table test, Valsalva, autonomic reflex screen, beat-to-beat BP monitoring
Efferent failureMSA, Parkinson disease, neurogenic autonomic failureImpaired sympathetic transduction and vascular resistanceSupine-upright BP/HR, plasma norepinephrine (supine vs upright), QSART, tilt-table
Vasovagal syncopePain, emotion, prolonged standing, heat, dehydrationInitial adrenergic rise followed by vagal predominance and hypotension/bradycardiaTilt-table provocation, orthostatic vitals, ECG/rhythm evaluation

Insular seizure as a great mimicker

  • Insular seizures can closely mimic reflex syncope.
  • Epigastric rising sensation is a key clinical clue.
  • Ictal EEG may show suppression rather than clear epileptiform discharge.

Medication focus

ScenarioMedication list
Catamenial seizureAcetazolamide, natural progesterone, medroxyprogesterone (do not list lamotrigine in this focused section)
Vasovagal / neurogenic orthostatic hypotensionMidodrine, Droxidopa, fludrocortisone

entries.title: 頭暈評估與頸動脈超音波適應症

S: 慢性頭暈合併頸部痠痛或姿勢改變後加重，且常描述為不穩感而非旋轉感。
反覆短暫旋轉感、翻身誘發，最常見周邊原因是 BPPV。
反覆眩暈合併偏頭痛史、畏光、畏聲或視覺先兆時，需考慮前庭型偏頭痛。
擔心頸動脈狹窄造成頭暈而要求做頸動脈超音波。
O: 頸因性頭暈診斷以排除為主，神經學缺損、HINTS、聽力與前庭檢查需整合判讀。
BPPV 以位置誘發眼振（如 Dix-Hallpike）支持診斷並可床邊復位。
頸動脈狹窄造成缺血性中風主要機轉是斑塊破裂後血栓栓塞，而非單純低灌流。
孤立性頭暈接受頸動脈超音波，臨床可處置之重大狹窄檢出率通常偏低。
A: 頸因性頭暈（CGD）常用解釋為頸部本體感覺與前庭/視覺輸入不一致，但其獨立疾病地位仍具爭議。
替代機制包含疼痛相關中樞敏化、姿勢控制網路失調與焦慮-過度警覺互相放大。
BPPV 是最常見可治療的周邊眩暈病因，應先辨識。
前庭型偏頭痛盛行率約 1–3%，可表現為自發或姿勢相關眩暈並伴偏頭痛特徵。
P: CGD 先治療頸部疼痛與活動受限，搭配前庭復健與姿勢訓練，不建議僅依單一影像下結論。
BPPV 以耳石復位術為主；長期規律使用止暈藥對周邊眩暈缺乏持續效益。
頸動脈超音波建議用於有局灶神經缺損、TIA/中風徵象、頸雜音或高動脈粥樣硬化風險族群。
前庭型偏頭痛治療包含生活型態調整與預防藥物；flunarizine 可作為預防選項之一。

versions.simple_zh:
頭暈要不要做頸動脈超音波？先看這 4 件事

頭暈很常見，但不是每次都要做頸動脈超音波。先分清楚頭暈型態，才能做對檢查。

1) 先辨認頭暈類型

常見類型特徵常見處置
BPPV（耳石脫落）翻身、抬頭誘發短暫旋轉感耳石復位術，通常改善很快
前庭型偏頭痛眩暈合併偏頭痛、怕光怕吵、視覺先兆生活作息調整＋預防藥物
頸因性頭暈（CGD）常伴頸痛、姿勢改變時不穩感加重頸部復健＋前庭訓練＋姿勢訓練

2) 什麼情況比較需要做頸動脈超音波？

  • 有單側無力、說話不清、臉歪等中風/TIA 警訊
  • 醫師聽到頸部血管雜音
  • 本身有高風險動脈粥樣硬化因素（高齡、糖尿病、吸菸等）

只有頭暈、沒有局灶神經症狀時，頸動脈超音波通常檢出率不高。

3) 重要觀念

頸動脈狹窄導致中風，主要機轉是血栓栓塞，不是單純「血流稍少」就一定頭暈。

4) 何時要急診？

  • 突然單側肢體無力或麻木
  • 說話困難、視力突然改變
  • 新發劇烈頭痛、步態明顯不穩
versions.professional_zh:
頭暈評估與頸動脈超音波適應症

頭暈評估應先完成分型與神經學危險訊號篩查，再決定是否安排頸動脈超音波。

病理與鑑別重點

  • 頸因性頭暈（Cervicogenic Dizziness, CGD）：與頸椎本體感覺輸入失衡、頸部疼痛導致的中樞感覺整合失調、深層頸屈肌控制下降及姿勢控制網路失衡相關；臨床上多為排除診斷，常見「頸痛＋非旋轉性不穩感」並隨頸部活動加重。
  • 良性陣發性姿勢性眩暈（Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo, BPPV）：位置改變誘發短暫旋轉感，Dix-Hallpike 與復位反應具高度診斷價值。
  • 前庭型偏頭痛（Vestibular Migraine）：可呈自發或姿勢性眩暈，常合併偏頭痛特徵（畏光、畏聲、先兆或偏頭痛病史）。

頸動脈超音波：何時有價值？

情境建議理由
疑似 TIA/中風、局灶神經缺損建議檢查可影響再灌流與二級預防策略
頸部雜音或高動脈粥樣硬化風險可考慮檢查有助斑塊與狹窄分層
孤立性頭暈、無神經定位徵象不建議常規篩檢可處置重大狹窄檢出率低

治療原則

  • CGD：結合頸部疼痛控制、關節活動度重建、深層頸屈肌訓練、前庭復健與姿勢控制再訓練。
  • 周邊眩暈：避免長期固定使用前庭抑制劑，以免延遲中樞代償。
  • 前庭型偏頭痛：生活型態管理 + 預防藥物（如 flunarizine）個別化使用。
versions.english:
Dizziness Evaluation and Carotid Duplex: Clinical Indications

Dizziness should be phenotyped first; carotid duplex is not a routine test for every dizzy patient.

Structured differential diagnosis

ConditionTypical cluesPractical first step
Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV，良性陣發性姿勢性眩暈)Brief positional spinning sensation when turning in bed or looking upPerform positional testing and canalith repositioning maneuvers
Vestibular Migraine（前庭型偏頭痛）Episodic vertigo with migraine features (photophobia, phonophobia, aura, or migraine history)Trigger/lifestyle control and individualized preventive therapy
Cervicogenic Dizziness (CGD，頸因性頭暈)Neck pain/stiffness with non-spinning disequilibrium that worsens with neck movementExclude central/vascular causes, then combine cervical and vestibular rehabilitation

CGD pathophysiology (clinical model)

  • Mismatch between abnormal cervical proprioceptive input and vestibular/visual signals.
  • Pain-driven central sensitization and altered sensorimotor integration.
  • Impaired deep neck flexor control and postural strategy instability.

CGD remains a diagnosis of exclusion; supportive findings include neck pain-linked disequilibrium and symptom reproduction with cervical movement.

When to order carotid duplex

  • Focal neurologic deficits or suspected TIA/stroke
  • Carotid bruit or high atherosclerotic burden

In isolated dizziness without focal signs, the diagnostic yield for actionable carotid stenosis is usually low.

Clinical pearl

Stroke related to carotid disease is predominantly thromboembolic, not simply due to mild isolated hypoperfusion.

versions.simple_zh:
物理治療疼痛管理指引

慢性疼痛的物理治療以規律運動為核心，各種儀器療法（電療、透熱、超音波）多為短期輔助，部分在隨機對照試驗中未顯示優於假治療的效益。

各儀器療法摘要

療法效益概述
微波透熱（Microwave Diathermy）慢性疼痛療效證據不足，不建議常規使用。
短波透熱（Shortwave Diathermy）慢性下背痛及退化性膝關節炎均無優於假治療的獲益，不建議常規推薦。
紅外線治療（Infrared Therapy）目前文獻未直接評估其在肌肉骨骼疼痛的療效，使用依據有限。
治療性超音波（Therapeutic Ultrasound）慢性疼痛及慢性下背痛療效不足，肌腱病變系統性回顧多顯示與假治療相差無幾。
TENS（經皮神經電刺激，Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation）不確定效益；退化性膝關節炎對照假治療，無顯著效益，有安慰劑作用；下背痛不建議常規使用。原發性痛經有高頻優於低頻之證據。

慢性下背痛

  • 首選：規律運動治療（型態依可近性與偏好）。
  • 短期輔助治療：表層熱療、手法治療、針灸或按摩。
  • 不建議：TENS（經皮神經電刺激）、治療性超音波、短波透熱（Shortwave Diathermy）。

退化性膝關節炎

  • 首選：低衝擊有氧 + 下肢肌力訓練；太極、瑜伽可作為輔助運動選項。
  • 輔助：局部熱療（短期症狀改善，缺乏強效試驗支持）。
  • 不建議：TENS（對照假治療，無顯著效益，有安慰劑作用）、短波透熱（Shortwave Diathermy）。
versions.professional_zh:
物理治療疼痛管理指引

基於現有實證彙整：慢性疼痛處置應以主動式運動復健為核心，各種物理儀器療法定位為短期輔助，多數在隨機試驗中未顯示優於假治療的一致性效益。

一、各療法療效與臨床建議（依適應症分類）

療法適應症 / 疾病療效訊號臨床建議

（Shortwave Diathermy）		 慢性下背痛 隨機試驗中缺乏一致性獲益 不建議常規使用
短波透熱
（Shortwave Diathermy）		 退化性膝關節炎 在教育加運動計畫中對照假治療，無顯著效益，有安慰劑作用 不建議常規使用
紅外線治療
（Infrared Therapy）		 肌肉骨骼疼痛 文獻未直接評估此適應症；現有依據有限 肌骨疼痛使用依據未建立
治療性超音波
（Therapeutic Ultrasound）		 慢性疼痛、慢性下背痛 療效不足 不建議常規使用
治療性超音波
（Therapeutic Ultrasound）		 肌腱病變 系統性回顧顯示療效邊際或與安慰劑相當 可作為深層熱療輔助；各熱療方式疼痛緩解療效相近

（Therapeutic Ultrasound）		 退化性膝關節炎 可攜式超音波有初步證據，但需長時間每日使用且費用偏高 可考慮但需評估成本效益
TENS
（經皮神經電刺激，
Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation）		 慢性疼痛 效益不確定；低證據品質；主要短期效益，長期療效不確定 可作為侷限性慢性疼痛的輔助選項，應設定謙遜預期值
TENS 退化性膝關節炎 對照假治療，無顯著效益，有安慰劑作用 不建議常規使用
TENS 原發性痛經 高頻 TENS 優於低頻之支持證據 高頻 TENS 可作為輔助選項
TENS 癌症相關疼痛 試驗與系統性回顧結果多為陰性或不足 不建議常規使用
TENS 急性疼痛 適切劑量下或有助益 可考慮短期使用；不支持慢性疼痛長期使用

二、慢性下背痛（Chronic Low Back Pain）

  • 核心：規律運動治療為首選，多數運動型態療效相近，選擇依可近性與病人偏好
  • 短期症狀輔助：表層熱療（含急性惡化期）；手法治療、針灸、按摩可短期改善，建議短期輔助主動治療
  • 心理社會高風險：建議合併認知行為治療（CBT，Cognitive Behavioral Therapy）或跨專業疼痛管理計畫
  • 不建議常規推薦：TENS（經皮神經電刺激）、治療性超音波、短波透熱（Shortwave Diathermy）——隨機試驗缺乏一致性效益

三、退化性膝關節炎（Knee Osteoarthritis）

  • 核心：低衝擊有氧 + 下肢肌力訓練；太極、瑜伽可作為補充運動選項
  • 物理治療轉介目的：優化運動計畫、個別化依損傷與偏好調整
  • 輔助症狀調節：局部熱療有短期疼痛效益，但缺乏強效試驗支持；部分病人在急性期或腫脹時使用冰敷可能暫時有幫助
  • 不建議：TENS（對照假治療，無顯著效益，有安慰劑作用）；短波透熱（Shortwave Diathermy，在教育加運動計畫中對照假治療無效益）

四、決策原則

  • 以功能恢復與活動參與為主要治療終點，不以單次止痛感受取代長期目標
  • 儀器療法可短期改善症狀，但不應取代運動與行為介入
  • 對高心理社會風險患者，建議納入認知行為治療（CBT，Cognitive Behavioral Therapy／認知行為治療）或跨專業疼痛管理計畫
versions.english:
Physical Therapy for Pain Management: Evidence-Based Guidelines

Based on current evidence synthesis: exercise-based rehabilitation is the core of chronic pain management; physical modalities serve as short-term adjuncts with variable or uncertain benefit.

Modality Summary

ModalityEfficacy SignalClinical Role
Microwave DiathermyInsufficient evidence of effectiveness for chronic pain.Not recommended as routine chronic pain treatment.
Shortwave DiathermyFor chronic low back pain: little evidence of consistent benefit from RCTs. For knee OA: no added benefit vs. sham in exercise program.Listed among therapies not routinely recommended.
Infrared TherapyCurrent evidence did not directly address infrared therapy as a PT pain modality for musculoskeletal conditions.Use case not established from retrieved content.
Therapeutic Ultrasound (low and high frequency)Insufficient evidence for chronic pain; systematic reviews for tendinopathy suggest marginal or no benefit vs. placebo. Wearable ultrasound has emerging evidence for knee OA but requires prolonged daily wear.Adjunct heat modality; evidence does not support routine use for chronic pain.
TENS (Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation)Uncertain benefit for chronic pain. Knee OA sham-controlled trials: no added benefit. Low back pain: not routinely recommended. Primary dysmenorrhea: high-frequency TENS shows evidence of benefit.Adjunct option with tempered expectations for localized chronic pain; not supported for long-term chronic pain management.

Chronic Low Back Pain

  • Core: Regular exercise therapy; most exercise types are similarly effective.
  • Adjuncts: Superficial heat for short-term relief; passive therapies (manipulation, acupuncture, massage) as short-term adjuncts to active therapy.
  • Avoid: TENS, therapeutic ultrasound, shortwave diathermy — little evidence of consistent benefit from RCTs.

Knee Osteoarthritis

  • Core: Low-impact aerobic training + lower-limb strengthening; tai chi and yoga as complementary options.
  • Adjuncts: Local heat (short-term benefit, lacks robust trial evidence).
  • Avoid: TENS (sham-controlled trials showed no added benefit, evidence of placebo component); shortwave diathermy (no added benefit vs. sham).

Ticagrelor 合併 Aspirin 於輕型缺血性中風／高風險 TIATHALES 研究納入 11,016 位輕型至中度非心因性缺血性中風（NIHSS ≤5）或高風險 TIA 病人。30 天主要終點（中風或死亡）於 ticagrelor-aspirin 組為 5.5%，aspirin 單藥組為 6.6%（HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.71–0.96）。

缺血性中風事件降低（5.0% vs 6.3%），但嚴重出血增加（0.5% vs 0.1%）。臨床應以「再缺血風險」與「出血風險」平衡決策，並排除需抗凝之心因性中風來源。

English Version

Ticagrelor in stroke

THALES trial randomized 11,016 patients with mild-to-moderate acute noncardioembolic ischemic stroke (NIHSS ≤5) or high-risk TIA

Primary efficacy outcome (stroke or death at 30 days): 5.5% with ticagrelor-aspirin vs 6.6% with aspirin alone (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.71-0.96, p=0.02). This represents an absolute risk reduction of 1.1%, with a number needed to treat of 92. [1]

Ischemic stroke: 5.0% with ticagrelor-aspirin vs 6.3% with aspirin alone (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.68-0.93, p=0.004). [1]

Major hemorrhage: Major ischemic events (ischemic stroke or nonhemorrhagic death) occurred in 5.3% with ticagrelor-aspirin vs 6.5% with aspirin alone (absolute risk reduction 1.19%). However, major hemorrhage (intracranial hemorrhage or hemorrhagic death) occurred in 0.4% with ticagrelor-aspirin vs 0.1% with aspirin alone (absolute risk increase 0.29%). [2] Severe bleeding overall occurred in 0.5% vs 0.1% (p=0.001), with a number needed to harm of 263.

The treatment effect of ticagrelor-aspirin accrued primarily over the first 10 days,

A network meta-analysis found Clopidogrel-aspirin ranked highest in SUCRA analysis and was associated with lower risk of functional disability compared to both aspirin alone and ticagrelor-aspirin
